question: What are the factors hindering on-site deployments of construction robots?

answer.answer:
On site, the factors that hold robots back are regulatory and legal approval (RI18), site constraints that limit where a machine can position itself and plan a path (RI5, PR12), the training burden on the workforce (RI6), work safety exposure (RI20) and the delivery model and work culture around the job (RI12); mobility (AT9) is the one property the literature says gets a robot onto the site at all. The sharpest point is upstream of all of these: the literature holds that on-site digital fabrication (PR8) presupposes a structured, controlled environment, the Mobile factory (CO12), and only one of the 50 coded cases draws on that condition, so the cure most often cited is also the least practised. The hindrances are also very unequal, with training drawn on by 44 of the 50 cases and the regulatory dependency carried by only 2, so an answer that lists them flat would mislead. Note too that on-site digital fabrication itself is drawn on by just 9 of the 50, and that significant human involvement (RE6) is present in all 50, meaning no deployed record in this set removes people from the site.

**The cited requirement that almost nothing meets**

PR8 "On-site DFAB" (Process) carries 1 inbound and 2 outbound dependency edges, and 9 of the 50 coded cases draw on it. [1] Its one precondition is the hardest: DEP41 states that PR8 hasPrecondition CO12 "Mobile factory" (Condition), backed by peer-reviewed evidence and carried by 1 of the 50 coded cases, on the argument that environments need to be much more structured and controlled before construction robots can take over. [1] CO12 itself is drawn on by 1 of the 50. [1] Read in the direction the relation gives, the controlled enclosure is upstream of on-site fabrication, and the record shows the Japanese industry has largely gone the other way: it deploys bare machines into unstructured sites instead. The same condition's own downstream claims are unexhibited: CO12 enablesCapability PR4 "Robotic assembly" is carried by 0 of the 50 [1], and CO12 amplifies VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency" is likewise carried by 0 of the 50 [1].

The counterweight is mobility. DEP86 has AT9 "Mobile" (Attribute) enablesCapability PR8, peer-reviewed, carried by 9 of the 50 coded cases, on the basis that a mobile robot with autonomous repositioning and localisation performs on-site digital fabrication [1], and AT9 is drawn on by 28 of the 50 [1]. Of PR8's two cited relations in that direction, mobility is carried as often as PR8 is drawn on, while the enclosed-factory condition is carried once.

**Regulatory and legal exposure**

DEP84 has PR8 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" (Risk), evidence graded as standard, carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases, with on-site 3D concrete printing proceeding via the IBC Section 104.11 alternative-means approval pathway [1]. The same risk sits under collaborative work: DEP45 has CO6 "Human-robot interaction" dependsOn RI18, standard evidence, carried by 2 of the 50, on compliance with robot safety standards [1]. RI18 is drawn on by 12 of the 50 and carries 5 cited edges in total, of which 2 appear here [1], so I cannot say how many further paths reach it.

**Site constraints and the limits on path-planning**

DEP44 has RI5 "Location dependent/site constraint" (Risk) constrains PR12 "Path-planning" (Process), peer-reviewed, carried by 15 of the 50 coded cases, because reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors, which constrains the choice of localisation method. [1] RI5 is drawn on by 21 of the 50 [1] and PR12 by 26 of the 50 [1]. This is the clearest mechanism in the retrieved material for why a machine that works in a factory bay stalls in a real building.

**Training, safety and the organisational setting**

RI6 "Require workforce training" is drawn on by 44 of the 50 coded cases [1], far more than any other hindrance here. DEP100 has AR9 "Automated production workflow" dependsOn RI6, peer-reviewed, carried by 38 of the 50, on the ground that the sophistication of digital technologies prohibits adoption by less technologically familiar workers [1], and DEP34 has CO6 "Human-robot interaction" dependsOn RI6, carried by 27 of the 50, since human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [1].

RI20 "Work safety concern" carries 3 inbound and 0 outbound edges, all listed, and is drawn on by 13 of the 50. [1] All three inbound edges are mitigations rather than causes: CO6 mitigates RI20, standard evidence, carried by 4 of the 50, through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation [1]; CO2 "3D scanning/RFID/sensing" mitigates RI20, standard evidence, carried by 7 of the 50, via speed-and-separation monitoring [1]; AT10 "Human assistance" mitigates RI20, peer-reviewed, carried by 8 of the 50, on exoskeleton evidence of an 11 to 33 per cent reduction in lumbar erector spinae activity [1]. So safety on site is addressed in the literature by sensing and by collaborative-robot limits, each carried by fewer than a sixth of the cases.

On the organisational side, DEP61 has PR4 "Robotic assembly" dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture" (Risk), peer-reviewed, carried by 2 of the 50, because robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [1], with RI12 drawn on by 16 of the 50 [1]. The contractual counter-move is barely present: AT13 "Risk-sharing/agile contracting" (Attribute) is drawn on by 2 of the 50 and carries no dependency edges [1], while CO11 "Early contractor involvement" is drawn on by 14 of the 50 [1], its cited edges running to off-site work rather than to on-site deployment: CO11 enablesCapability PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", carried by 13 of the 50 [1].

**What the deployed record shows**

The on-site cases here are mobile machines working in the open, not enclosed factories. census_RXI5-1, developed by Firm_081, was adopted to address digital, safety and integration, performs digging, heavy lift and material handling on sitework, at technology readiness level 8 [2]. RP12 addresses labour and integration, performs digging and material handling on sitework, deployed as a mobile robot on site outdoors, at technology readiness level 9. [3] RP11 works on the structural core as a mobile robot on site outdoors, at technology readiness level 7 [4], and RP24 performs drilling on interior fitout and services as a mobile robot, indoors and on site, at technology readiness level 8 [5].

Readiness also varies within a single task in the welding records. census_RXM4-2, from Firm_115, was adopted to address cost and labour, performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core, at technology readiness level 7 [6], whereas census_RXH3-2, from Firm_143, performs the same assembly, steelwork and welding at technology readiness level 9 [7]. A similar split shows in simpler work: census_RXH5-4, from Firm_027, Firm_028 and Firm_033, addresses labour and performs cleaning at technology readiness level 9 [8], while census_RXM30-1, from Firm_034, Firm_088 and Firm_089, performs assembly, erection and steelwork on the structural core and sitework at technology readiness level 7 [9]. The context does not state which enablers any of these cases draws on, so these readiness figures stand as the record of deployment, not as evidence for a particular edge.

**What edge-walking would miss**

RE6 "Significant human involvement" is drawn on by 50 of the 50 coded cases and has no cited dependency edge at all [1], so the most consistent fact about these deployments, that a person is still in the loop, has not been connected by the literature. An enabler with no edge is present and usable: the evidence for it is how many of the 50 cases draw on it and what it co-occurs with. [1] As correlation only, RE6 co-occurs with AR9 "Automated production workflow" in 44 cases and with VA13 "Improve site safety" in 39 [1]. The cited dependency layer is sparse: 100 edges touching 68 of the 140 enablers [1] and 60% of Risks carry none [1], so the hindrances listed above are those the literature has connected, and the retrieved material does not establish that they are the complete set.

**Deployed evidence.** Selected by filtering the coded records, not by similarity. 13 records in the graph carry onsite as their deployment setting; all are listed below.
- RP1, adopted to address cost, labor, integration; performs 3d printing, concrete work; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP11, adopted to address digital; performs assembly, concrete work, rebar, steelwork; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP12, adopted to address labor, integration; performs digging, material handling; works on sitework; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP13, adopted to address digital; performs surveying & mapping; works on sitework; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP14, adopted to address cost, safety, labor; performs heavy lift, material handling; works on sitework; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP17, adopted to address digital, quality; performs inspection; works on the building envelope, the facade, or curtain wall; deployed on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP18, adopted to address quality, labor; performs steelwork, surface, surface treatment; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP19, adopted to address labor; performs concrete work, finishing, surface treatment; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP20, adopted to address digital, labor; performs assembly, surface treatment; works on the interior fitout; deployed as a mobile robot, indoors, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP21, adopted to address digital; performs material handling; works on sitework; deployed off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP22, adopted to address cost, market; performs 3d printing, assembly, material handling; works on sitework, the building envelope, the facade, or curtain wall; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP24, adopted to address digital; performs drilling; works on the interior fitout, services, mep; deployed as a mobile robot, indoors, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP25, adopted to address labor; performs cleaning, material handling; deployed on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
